confirmed_defects.finding: The same Wen Zhi changes from he/him/man to she/her/woman without a change of person or explained transition, while the six tubs, T4, late brother and workshop remain identical.

evidence.text: The crew fitted the higher tackle while Sui Yan supervised the handling precautions. The tubs had been cleared for controlled movement, but residue on the lower surfaces still required protection and separation. An ordinary worker read each container mark aloud to the inventory clerk. Wen Zhi stood in the public viewing place with his old maker's drawing. Miao stood beside him, holding the merchant's invoices. Their rivalry had become a strange partnership of watching. Each feared the other's tub would disappear under a description nobody could challenge afterward.

Wen showed an older maker's mark cut by his brother. He kept the drawing because memory became unreliable after death. His brother died years earlier from fever; tools passed through ordinary family division. Wen chose containers over boats because they stayed in one place. T4's ordeal offended that reason as well as his account. He Ming listened gently. The private story did not enlarge accepted damages or change title. It made the man at the angry window easier to understand. Yue saw how many people's practical choices were built around grief no public notice ever had reason to explain.

The first evacuation group came from three low workshops. Wen Zhi walked beside her empty tubs, which remained stacked at her own premises after their earlier return. She had chosen to leave them on a raised platform rather than pay somebody to carry six bulky containers into a crowded shelter. She wore her brother's old scarf and disliked how pleased a neighbor looked to offer help. At the lane entrance she stopped to check that the workshop lock had caught. Yan gave her time to look from the safe side. Then she left, without taking the risk back.

At Wen's workshop, the ordinary rack held a sound modest load. Yue had come by invitation to drink tea, not inspect the repair after its claim closed. Wen asked whether the traveler wanted a tub as a parting gift. Yue stared until the woman laughed. She had chosen the largest container for the joke. The habitual pack could not contain it, and no gift was actually offered. They drank tea and discussed Wen's next private order. The workshop would stay busy after the public case became somebody else's story. Wen hoped it became a shorter story soon.

repairs.before: Across the quay, Wen Zhi found water beneath two stacked tubs and a crack in the workshop door frame. The containers themselves were sound. Her late brother's maker marks looked darker when wet, as if somebody had recently cut them. She cleaned them with the cloth he once used and disliked the sudden memory. Peng Li had a paid repair slot available after his current job. Wen accepted the quote, then asked him to leave the old hinge if it still worked. He examined it and said it did. An original thing could remain without pretending damage had never happened.

repairs.before: Peng's plane came from the same lender who had approved its earlier use, under a renewed ordinary loan with a return day. Yue saw him carrying it wrapped against the remaining rain. He complained that the harbor was now full of doors wanting attention at the same time. She asked which door was least patient. He said every owner believed it was theirs. Wen overheard and said hers had been waiting decades for a carpenter with manners. The three of them laughed. Nobody needed the joke to settle the price or transfer a borrowed tool into anyone's permanent pack.

evidence.text: The clinic assistant met them at the shelter. The boy was conscious but shivering violently, his wet clothes stiffening at the edges. She directed the team to move him gently into the warmer room, remove the wet layers with privacy, and use the available dry insulation while she assessed him. Nobody asked him to explain himself first. His grandmother sat outside the screen, gripping the spare rope so tightly that Lin had to offer her a cloth before the strands cut her palm.

In the clinic, the boy slept through the morning while his grandmother counted the knots in the spare rope. The assistant had checked him repeatedly overnight. His alertness and warmth had improved, but the toes injured by cold would need time before their recovery could be judged. Lin brought breakfast for the grandmother from the ordinary family-support allotment. The old woman ate standing until the assistant pointed firmly at the chair. Lin recognized the gesture from Shi Lan's lunches.

The child injured in the earlier ditch fall came to the clinic for her scheduled review. He could walk farther now, but the affected foot still ached after cold journeys. The clinician changed her ordinary protection and activity advice, explaining which symptoms required another visit. His father asked whether the spring road would solve it. The clinician said warmer weather could help without promising an exact end to pain. Lin brought the family their accepted next wood-carrying slot. The child showed Lin a paper bird with one wing wider than the other and said it flew best sideways.

confirmed_defects.fix: Use his for both references to the boy.

confirmed_defects.finding: The child is discharged and living at home in Book XIII section10, then returns for ordinary checks in11; section12 repeats first discharge and need for a larger boot without any intervening readmission, although that boot is already in use.

evidence.text: At the clinic, the boy was cleared for discharge under an ordinary home-care plan when the household could provide warmth, clean dressings, and the advised reduced movement. His grandmother and mother arranged those conditions with the assistant. He would return for checks; lasting damage to the toes remained uncertain. Wen delivered the larger boot's fitting appointment, which would wait until swelling settled. The boy asked whether that meant he had to remain barefoot forever. The assistant said forever was not today's instruction.

Lin helped carry the family's bags for the homeward cart, leaving the medical tasks to those assigned. The boy sat wrapped beside his grandmother and waved at the paper dog, whose guardian had reclaimed it after the visit. The niece waved the dog back. The cart moved by the safe lower route. In the shelter, the closed shortcut board stayed where it belonged. A child going home did not make the ditch repaired. It did make the clinic room ready for the next person needing warmth.

Before the convoy week, Long visited the boy's household to ask whether the borrowed handcart had met the revised carrier demand. He brought the clerk responsible for its schedule, ready to hear the practical answer. The grandmother said the cart worked and the first loading point still grew icy. The clerk noted the need for grit there. The boy showed Long his new larger boot, not yet worn outside. Long admired it with the solemnity he usually gave scales.

At the clinic, the boy from the ditch had returned for his scheduled check. He recognized the new patient as a driver because of the dust on his coat and wanted to hear about the wagon. The assistant permitted a short conversation after both were settled. The driver described the horse rather than the nearly overturned grain. The boy described his larger boot. They compared injuries with the grave competitiveness of people whose immediate universe had narrowed to a badly behaved limb.

At the clinic, the cold-injured boy was finally preparing to go home under the assistant's plan. His warmth and general condition were stable, but the foot still needed protected care and a larger soft boot. The family received the actual follow-up dates and warning signs, not a declaration that winter had left no mark. The grandmother had arranged the stove help and carried wood turn. Lin brought the paper dog with the niece's renewed permission, and the boy gave it a place beside the boot.

When the boy left the clinic, the assistant's paid family-support turn ended under its terms. Home care continued through the family's own arrangements and the scheduled follow-up. The grandmother carried the instructions in a covered fold, the same hands that had once clenched the rope now careful with a page. Lin helped move the bedding to the cart. The boy waved from his wrapped seat. She waved back, relieved enough to feel the remaining uncertainty more sharply rather than less.

confirmed_defects.fix: Describe a completed scheduled followup and return home with his existing larger boot; keep continuing medical limits and transport conditions.

evidence.text: From the lower shoulder Yue saw a small handcart tipped beside a shallow crack. One wheel pointed upward; its other side lay below the salt lip. A woman sat beneath its frame, shading her eyes with a folded cloth. Farther west a man knelt beside a patch of dark crust. He raised an arm when Tuo called, then lowered it as if the gesture had used his remaining strength. There were no animals, no magical barrier, no wall of enemies. The distance to them looked short. The ground between them looked like more of the road.

He examined the patient himself, checked circulation and sensation, then discussed transport with her. Bao agreed that he could take over. He promised to keep it supported and obtain fuller examination in Bitter Wells. That answer steadied the woman more than Han's earlier hopeful silence. Bao gave him the written treatment record and sufficient copies for the town clinic and the patient. Tuo handed the older guide his recovered notebook.

The farrier led the mules to the established trough, where the keeper checked that the water was running clean from the town service. The crew's travelling stock stood untouched while people recovered their breath. Gao kept her field case on the high bench away from the washing splash. When the keeper asked whether the expedition had found the lost palace, she said they had found a store with a name, a road with a warning, and two men who wanted to be home. He decided this was a better result.

evidence.text: Her palms had healed, but she still avoided taking a loaded rope or forcing the damaged joint with her shoulder. The task required ordinary hands, a clear view, and the tool's known fit. Han steadied the box beside the wheel. The stream thinned, then stopped. Nobody celebrated until the driver checked the brake again and the farrier examined the collar for a renewed drip. Rain ticked against the empty pot lid. The ground had received more water than their margin wanted to spare. Yue's task was to keep the loose cover from whipping across the farrier's face.

Then he tested the shutter's lower edge with a plain timber wedge, keeping force away from the brittle surrounding plaster. It shifted a little. The conservator put a sheet beneath the gap to catch loose material without letting it blow into the room. Yue steadied the sheet's outside corner at her direction. The mason let Yue brush loose grit from the wedge's working place using the small plain brush he lent her. Her healed palms tolerated the light task; she did not grip the wedge or brace the shutter.
